notes: Demo files are stored in Git LFS (see .gitattributes). Clone with `git lfs install` first, or the .dem files arrive as ~130-byte pointer stubs.

Per D5, every entry records how its era was established. Date demos from seasonal asset names in their string tables, never from protocol numbers - protocol 3 / network 24 spans at least 2015 through 2026 and dates nothing.
Reproduce any field below with `python tools/inspect_demo.py walk|date <file>`.

Asset dating works better on older demos than newer ones, which is convenient given that older demos are the ones hardest to date otherwise. Competitive players bought heavily early in TF2's life - unusuals were everywhere until people noticed the visual noise was a competitive disadvantage with no upside - so early comp demos carry plenty of dated cosmetics. A modern comp demo like serveme-627619 carries almost none, which is why its asset dating yields only ' 2019 or later' against a true date of 2026.

The era axis now has three specimens with exact, externally established dates - protocol 14 (2008), 15 (2009) and 24 (2013) - each recorded on a period client whose `version` command reports its build. Everything else is 2020 or later at protocol 24. The remaining gap is protocols 16-23, the Source Multiplayer era from October 2011 to some point before March 2013, which no corpus file covers; four protocol-conditional rules are still unexecuted on their far side. A build filling it must be stamped between those dates, and `Exe build` in bin/engine.dll reads that stamp without launching anything.

demos.source: recorded by the owner 2026-08-10 on TF2 build 3420, from an archive.org retail Orange Box pack; extracted to F:\tf2-builds\tf2-2008
demos.eraEvidence: The client's own version command: `Protocol version 14`, `Exe version 1.0.2.2 (tf)`, `Exe build: 20:17:35 Mar 19 2008 (3420)`. Third corpus entry with an exact externally established date rather than an inferred lower bound, and the oldest specimen by five years.
demos.whyItMatters: The corpus's only protocol-14 file and its pre-Source-2009 anchor. It confirmed a pre-registered prediction (docs/TIMELINE.md): decodes end to end with zero stops while exercising the one branch that had never run against real data - the absent string table compression flag below PROTOCOL_VERSION_14, across 16 svc_CreateStringTable messages - plus 45 svc_Prefetch messages on the 13-bit index. Both rules existed only because proto_version.h said they should.
demos.knownIssues: None. 12,608 commands, 22,176 trace lines, no stops and no unknown or undecoded markers, frame check 2764 against 2764 declared.
demos.privacyNote: Carries a REAL Steam account id, unlike the 2009 and 2013 entries which record STEAM_0:0:0. The 2008 build refuses to start without a running Steam process, so the client had a logged-in session to write. Retained deliberately with the owner's consent - the id is already public on their ESEA profile. Redacting it was rejected because altering the bytes destroys the file's value as a faithful specimen.
demos.notes: Carries NO dem_stringtables command, where the 2009 and 2013 entries each carry exactly one. At protocol 14 the tables arrive only as svc_CreateStringTable in the signon stream. Not documented in proto_version.h and not predicted - the same discovery shape as RISKS B17 and B18. It also disproved a fingerprint: the string table COUNT is 16 here, in the 2009 demo and in modern demos alike, so it dates nothing. Max classes does move: 216 here, 232 in 2009, 275 modern.

demos.source: recorded by the owner 2026-08-09 on TF2 build 3862, from the archive.org 'team-fortress-2-3862' pack (see DECISIONS.md D19)

The only corpus entry with an exact, externally established date rather than an inferred lower bound.
demos.whyItMatters: The only pre-2020 demo and the only one below network protocol 24. It exercises five protocol-conditional rules on their old side simultaneously - the five-bit message type field, no svc_ServerInfo replay flag, a four-byte map CRC rather than a 16-byte hash, a 13-bit svc_Prefetch index, and fixed 20-bit string table lengths. Four of those had been written from reading demostf/parser and never executed; the fifth was not known to exist until this demo failed on it (RISKS B17).
demos.knownIssues: None. Decodes end to end with zero stops: 156 game event definitions, 10,998 entity snapshots, 70 game events across 13 types, and the recording player resolved by name from the userinfo table.
demos.privacyNote: Recorded on a listen server in insecure mode, so the userinfo record carries STEAM_0:0:0 rather than a real account id. clientName is the owner's public handle, which the repository already carries in its path.
demos.notes: Contrast tools/corpus/demos/etf2l-12025-pov-2020-07-21.dem: both are POV, eleven years apart. The pair is the closest thing this corpus has to a controlled comparison across the era axis.

demos.source: recorded by the owner 2026-08-10 on TF2 build 1729296, from an archive.org retail pack; extracted to F:\tf2-builds\tf2-2013
demos.eraEvidence: Not dated from assets - `tools/inspect_demo.py date` finds no seasonal assets at all, because a freshly recorded listen-server demo carries no cosmetics. It did not have to be: the client reports `Protocol version 24`, `Exe version 1729296 (tf)`, `Exe build: 17:24:29 Mar 25 2013 (5252) (215)`. The second corpus entry with an exact externally established date rather than an inferred lower bound, and the demonstration that asset dating and build dating are independent methods - this file is undatable by the first and exact under the second.
demos.whyItMatters: Establishes that network protocol 24 was already live on 2013-03-25, which puts the 23->24 change BEFORE that date and earlier than a SteamPipe-anchored guess would place it. It does not fill the corpus's real gap: protocols 16-23 remain unrepresented, and with them four protocol-conditional rules stay unexecuted on their far side. Its practical value is as a control - a protocol-24 demo of known provenance to compare against z1800.dem, whose exact recording date is unknown.
demos.knownIssues: None. Decodes end to end with zero stops: 16,499 commands, 44,007 trace lines, no unknown or undecoded markers, frame check 7838 against 7838 declared.
demos.privacyNote: Recorded on a listen server in insecure mode, so the userinfo record carries STEAM_0:0:0 rather than a real account id. clientName is the in-game display name that client was configured with.
demos.notes: This file found a real bug on first read. Its recording player's name contains a non-ASCII character, and the dump printed it two different ways in one output - `mia??ker` from the header, which read ASCII, and correctly from the userinfo table, which read UTF-8. Nothing failed; both were plausible names. Every string decoder is UTF-8 as of that fix, and the disagreement between two decoders was the only signal.

corpusGaps.preTwentyTwenty: EMPTY, and not for lack of trying. Checked 2026-08-07: RGL launched 2019 so its oldest demos are the same era as these. ETF2L's listing goes back to Sept 2014 but the files have rotted - every demo id below ~12010 returns HTTP 404, and the live floor is id 12025, dated 2020-07-23. ESEA's SourceTV demos shipped with expiry dates and were never permanently downloadable, so there is nothing to recover; community Mega collections catalogued on teamfortress.tv in 2013 are long dead. sizzlingstats, which did keep demos, is gone.
corpusGaps.consequence: The parser has no historical coverage and no test that would reveal its absence. See D5 - the schema-driven design has to be right by construction, because it cannot be verified.

verifiedButNotStored.why: These parse end to end and are recorded for auditability, but are not committed. Git LFS on the free tier allows 1 GB of storage and 1 GB of bandwidth per month; the stored corpus is already ~316 MB and every fresh clone spends that against the bandwidth allowance. Test value is per-map and per-quirk rather than per-file, and these five duplicate maps already covered.
